It should be noted that in the present design the participants are not residents of the neighborhoods they evaluate, so what varies is the baseline quality of the scene and not the observer's own environmental deprivation.
Participants were assigned to one of three neighborhood socioeconomic status levels (Low SES: n = 24; Medium SES: n = 26; High SES: n = 25).
All participants signed the informed consent prior to the start of the sessions.
Upon arrival at the laboratory, participants were received, compliance with inclusion criteria was verified, and they signed the corresponding informed consent.

Next, participants completed exposure to the second experimental condition under the same posture, body rotation, and oculomotor recording protocol, followed by a second administration of the questionnaire package.

Moreover, since participants were not residents of these neighborhoods, the results describe how scenes of different baseline quality respond to the same kind of intervention, and not the effect on people living in deprived environments.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample size was determined a priori through a power analysis in G*Power 3.1 for a mixed ANOVA 3 × 2 (one between-subjects factor: Neighborhood SES; one within-subject factor: Design Condition). Assuming a level α = .05, a power (1 -β) = .80, a correlation between repeated measures of .50, nonsphericity correction ε = 1, and a small-to-medium effect size of f = 0.20, the calculation indicated a minimum required sample of N = 66 participants (with df = 63 in the denominator for the Condition × SES interaction). To prevent loss of power derived from experimental mortality or oculomotor calibration failures, the sample was oversampled by 14%, reaching the target figure of 75 participants.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Biophilic Interventions Across Urban Socioeconomic Contexts: A VR and Eye-Tracking Study
table.research_questions:
RQ1. Does biophilic enhancement improve positive affect, liking, aesthetic evaluation, relaxation, and visual engagement compared to the original scene?
RQ2. Does this effect differ across Low-, Medium-, and High-SES neighborhoods?
RQ3. Are changes in visual attention associated with changes in affective and evaluative responses?
H1. Bio-enhanced scenes will produce higher positive affect, liking, aesthetic evaluation, relaxation, and visual engagement than Original scenes.
H2. The marginal benefit of bio-enhancement will be larger in Low-SES contexts (equigenesis prediction).
H3. Fixations in intervention areas will increase more strongly in Low-SES scenes.
H4. Bio-enhancement may increase positive affect and relaxation without immediately reducing perceived stress.
H5. Increases in visual exploration of biophilic elements will correlate with increases in positive affect.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Authors have observed the data, but have not performed the proposed analyses. At least some of the data that will be used for this analysis plan has been accessed and observed by the authors. The authors have sufficiently observed relevant evidence to influence their analysis decisions or conclusions. However, the authors have not yet performed any of the proposed analyses in this plan and will not do so until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Direct inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to infer or estimate a causal relationship between two or more variables. It is designed specifically for the purposes of causal inference or identification.
table.additional_blinding_during_research_or_a: No blinding procedures were used. Participants were not informed of the specific hypotheses. To minimize bias, no descriptive statistics, visualizations, or inferential analyses were conducted on the final dataset before registration. Eye-tracking metrics were extracted automatically, and all hypotheses and analysis plans were specified prior to any inferential testing of the final data.
table.stimuli_description: Participants viewed immersive VR tours composed of six sequential 360° videos from a single urban neighborhood (Low-, Medium-, or High-SES). Each participant viewed two versions of the same neighborhood: an Original condition and a Bio-enhanced condition. The order of conditions was randomized. Videos lasted approximately one minute each and contained 12 predefined Areas of Interest (AOIs) used for eye-tracking analyses. Eye movements were recorded throughout the VR exposure using the SightLab VR platform. After each condition, participants completed questionnaires assessing affective and evaluative responses.
table.inter_trial_interval: Not applicable. The study did not use discrete experimental trials. Participants viewed continuous VR tours consisting of six sequential 360° videos per condition, followed by questionnaire completion. A five-minute washout period with a neutral task was administered between the Original and Bio-enhanced conditions.
table.eye_tracker_type: For virtual reality eye tracking, data were collected using the integrated head-mounted eye tracker of the Meta Quest Pro (Type: mobile / head-mounted VR HMD; Manufacturer: Meta Platforms, Inc.; Model: Meta Quest Pro). Eye-tracking data were recorded throughout the exposure at a sampling frequency of 60 Hz and extracted via the SightLab VR platform (WorldViz).
table.display_screen_size: Not applicable (VR Head-Mounted Display). Visual stimuli were presented using the integrated dual Mini-LED LCD displays of the Meta Quest Pro headset, with a resolution of 1800 × 1920 pixels per eye, a Field of View (FOV) of 106° horizontal by 96° vertical, and a panel size of approximately 2.48 inches per eye (diagonal).
table.head_movement_restrictions: No head movement restrictions were used. Participants freely explored the immersive VR environment while viewing the 360° videos. Eye-tracking calibration relied on the headset's stored calibration profile with automatic slippage correction.
table.lighting_conditions: Participants were exposed to immersive 360° videos using a VR headset while standing. Eye tracking was recorded through the headset using the SightLab VR platform. Lighting conditions were not manipulated and were not a study variable.
table.immediate_surroundings: Participants stood during VR exposure and were allowed to rotate freely, although translational movement was restricted. If participants moved outside the central anchor area, they were verbally reminded to return to the center. They advanced through the virtual scenes using a controller.
table.calibration_points: Calibration was performed using the Meta Quest Pro's integrated system calibration procedure, which utilizes a 5-point calibration array (center, top, bottom, left, right). For the experimental sessions, eye-tracking used the headset's stored calibration profile with automatic slippage correction, with no forced recalibration per session. Initial accuracy was validated through the native Meta system check prior to testing, and recordings were subsequently screened for technical errors (such as tracker loss or calibration failure).
table.area_of_interest_design: Each 360° video contained 12 predefined Areas of Interest (AOIs). AOIs were manually defined within the immersive VR scenes and classified according to two independent dimensions: Original Scenery (OS) and Biophilic Intervention (BI). Across the six videos presented in each condition, participants viewed a total of 72 AOIs per condition. AOI size varied according to the characteristics of each area within the 360° environment and was not defined using a fixed pixel size.
table.size_of_aois: AOI size was not fixed. Areas of Interest (AOIs) were manually defined within each 360° video according to the content of the scene and varied in size depending on the intervention area represented. Fixed pixel dimensions were not applicable in the immersive VR environment.
table.distance_between_and_placement_of_aois: AOIs were embedded within immersive 360° VR scenes and corresponded to predefined elements of the urban environment. Their spatial location varied according to the content of each scene. AOIs were not arranged on a fixed 2D display grid, and therefore fixed distances or screen positions were not applicable.
table.randomization: Participants were assigned to one of three neighborhood socioeconomic status (SES) conditions (Low, Medium, or High) using a counterbalancing procedure to ensure approximately equal group sizes. Within each participant, the order of the two experimental conditions (Original vs. Bio-enhanced) was randomized using a simple randomization procedure. Each participant viewed both conditions of the same neighborhood, and the presentation order was randomized at the individual level. No blocking or stratification procedures were used.
table.explanation_of_foreknowledge_and_managin: Data collection was completed before registration, but no descriptive statistics, visualizations, or inferential analyses were conducted on the final dataset prior to registration. Raw eye-tracking data were extracted automatically and stored on a secure institutional server with restricted access. Hypotheses, confirmatory and exploratory distinctions, and the analysis plan were specified before any inferential testing of the final dataset. The pilot study was conducted on an independent dataset and was used only to inform the methodology and predictions.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants were recruited from the university community of the University of Almería via public advertisement on the university's online portal. The target population was adults (≥18 years) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Although recruitment was directed at the university community (students and staff), being a university student was not an inclusion requirement. All participants who responded were undergraduate students. Data were collected in Almería, Spain, between May 15 and June 30, 2026.

Inclusion criteria:
Participants were eligible if they: (1) were adults (≥18 years); (2) had normal or corrected-to-normal vision; (3) reported no history of severe motion sickness in VR; (4) reported no color blindness; (5) reported no neurological impairment; and (6) reported no other medical condition that could affect VR use or task performance (e.g., photosensitive epilepsy, vestibular disorders). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Exclusion criteria:
Participants were excluded a priori if they did not meet any of the inclusion criteria. No additional exclusion criteria were applied.

Procedure. 1. Recruitment and written informed consent. 2. Assignment to one SES neighborhood (counterbalanced across participants). 3. Eye-tracking used the headset's stored calibration profile with automatic slippage correction. No forced recalibration per session. 4. First condition (Original or Bio-enhanced, randomized): tour of six sequential 360° videos, roughly one minute each. 5. Eye-tracking recorded throughout at 60 Hz. 6. After the first tour, HMD removed and questionnaires completed (PANAS, ad-hoc items, qualitative questions). 7. Five-minute washout with a neutral task. 8. Second condition: same procedure with the other version. 9. Questionnaires again. 10. Debriefing.

Participants stood during the VR exposure. They could rotate freely on themselves, but translational movement was restricted. If they stepped outside the central anchor area defined by the system, they were verbally reminded to return to the center. They advanced through scenes with the controller.
table.sample_size: The final sample consisted of 75 participants. Participants were assigned to one of three Neighborhood SES groups: Low SES (n = 24), Medium SES (n = 26), and High SES (n = 25). The study used a mixed design, with Neighborhood SES as a between-subjects factor and Condition (Original vs. Bio-enhanced) as a within-subjects factor. All participants completed both conditions, resulting in repeated measurements nested within participants.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target sample size was determined a priori using G*Power 3.1 for a mixed-design ANOVA with one between-subjects factor (Neighborhood SES: Low, Medium, High) and one within-subjects factor (Condition: Original vs. Bio-enhanced). The analysis assumed α = .05, power = .80, a correlation among repeated measures of .50, a nonsphericity correction ε = 1, and an effect size of f = 0.20. The minimum required sample size was N = 66 participants. To account for potential attrition, incomplete eye-tracking recordings, calibration failures, missing questionnaire data, and other sources of data loss, the target sample size was increased by approximately 14%, resulting in a planned sample of N = 75 participants.
table.stopping_rule: A pilot study (N = 16) was conducted to validate the methodology and was treated as a separate dataset. The final study began after completion of the pilot phase. Data collection stopped when the predetermined target sample size of 75 participants was reached. No interim analyses or data-dependent stopping rules were used.
table.manipulated_variables:
Two variables were manipulated: 
1. Condition was a within-subjects factor with two levels: Original and Bio-enhanced. 
2. Neighborhood SES was a between-subjects factor with three levels: Low, Medium, and High. 
Each participant was assigned to one Neighborhood SES condition and viewed both conditions of the same neighborhood.
table.measured_variables:
The study included subjective, eye-tracking, and qualitative measures:  
Subjective measures were Positive Affect (PANAS), Negative Affect (PANAS), Liking, Relaxation, Aesthetic Evaluation, Perceived Stress, and Interest. These measures assessed participants' affective and evaluative responses to the virtual environments. Variable roles were specified a priori. Positive Affect (PANAS), Liking, Aesthetic Evaluation, Relaxation, Perceived Stress, Fixations in Intervention Areas, and Total Fixation Count were designated as confirmatory outcomes. Negative Affect (PANAS) was designated as a hypothesis-informed exploratory outcome. Interest, together with the remaining eye-tracking and qualitative variables, was designated as exploratory.

Eye-tracking measures included Total Fixation Count, Average Fixation Duration, Average Saccadic Velocity, Peak Saccadic Velocity, Average Saccadic Amplitude, Peak Saccadic Amplitude, Time to First Fixation, and First Fixation Duration. These metrics were used to characterize visual engagement, attention allocation, attentional orienting, and oculomotor behavior during exposure to the VR scenes.

Additional AOI-based measures included Fixations in Intervention Areas (Original condition) and Fixations in Intervention Areas (Bio-enhanced condition), reflecting attention directed toward areas targeted for intervention. In the Bio-enhanced condition, these fixation counts were further classified into Pure Biophilia Fixations, Urban Regeneration Fixations, Mixed Regeneration + Biophilia Fixations, and Artistic Biophilia Fixations, allowing assessment of visual attention to different intervention types.

Qualitative measures included Three Words, Positive Element, Negative Element, Preferred Version, Reason for Preference, and Comfort Version, which captured participants’ subjective impressions and preferences regarding the environments.
table.indices:
No composite indices were used. All variables are single measures as defined in the Variables section.

For correlational analyses, delta scores will be computed for variables measured in both conditions as:

Δ variable = Bio-enhanced − Original.

Specifically:

Δ Fixations in Intervention Areas = Fixations in Intervention Areas (Bio-enhanced condition) − Fixations in Intervention Areas (Original condition).

In addition, Fixations in Intervention Areas (Bio-enhanced condition) is defined as:

Fixations in Intervention Areas (Bio-enhanced condition) = Pure Biophilia Fixations + Urban Regeneration Fixations + Mixed Regeneration + Biophilia Fixations + Artistic Biophilia Fixations.

The four intervention subcomponents are mutually exclusive and exhaustive subsets of Fixations in Intervention Areas (Bio-enhanced condition).
table.eye_tracking_processing_algorithm: Raw eye-tracking data were processed using a velocity-threshold identification (I-VT) algorithm.
table.minimal_fixation_duration: Fixations were defined as gaze velocity below 30°/s for at least 100 ms.
table.upper_velocity_threshold: Fixations were defined as gaze velocity below 30°/s for at least 100 ms. Saccades were movements above that threshold.
table.gap_fill_in_functions_or_noise_reduction: No gap fill-in functions or noise reduction algorithms were specified.
table.eye_s_analyzed: Not specified. Eye-tracking metrics were extracted automatically by the SightLab VR platform.
table.statistical_tests:
The primary analyses will consist of mixed ANOVAs conducted separately for each confirmatory dependent variable. The within-subjects factor will be Condition (Original vs. Bio-enhanced), the between-subjects factor will be Neighborhood SES (Low, Medium, High), and SES_individual will be included as a covariate. The model will test the main effects of Condition and Neighborhood SES, the Condition × Neighborhood SES interaction, and exploratory effects involving the covariate. Separate models will be conducted for Positive Affect (PANAS), Liking, Aesthetic Evaluation, Relaxation, Perceived Stress, Fixations in Intervention Areas, and Total Fixation Count. For measures represented by Original and Bio-enhanced values (e.g., Total Fixation Count and Fixations in Intervention Areas), these two values constitute the within-subjects levels of Condition.
Negative Affect (PANAS) will be analyzed as a hypothesis-informed exploratory outcome using the same mixed ANOVA structure. Interest will be analyzed as an exploratory outcome using the same mixed ANOVA structure.

Exploratory mixed ANOVAs using the same factorial structure will be conducted for Average Fixation Duration and Average Saccadic Velocity. Separate one-way ANOVAs with Neighborhood SES as the between-subjects factor will be conducted for Pure Biophilia Fixations, Urban Regeneration Fixations, Mixed Regeneration + Biophilia Fixations, and Artistic Biophilia Fixations. If count distributions are severely non-normal, alternative count models (e.g., Poisson or negative binomial models) may be considered and reported as exploratory deviations.

Correlational analyses will be conducted using Pearson or Spearman correlations on delta scores (Bio-enhanced − Original). Confirmatory triangulation blocks will examine associations between changes in visual engagement and affective outcomes (H1), between Neighborhood SES and magnitude of change (H2), and between changes in average saccadic velocity, perceived stress, relaxation, and positive affect (H4). Additional hypothesis-informed exploratory correlations will evaluate associations between attention to intervention areas, biophilic fixation measures, average fixation duration, and affective and evaluative outcomes. Exploratory analyses involving Time to First Fixation and First Fixation Duration will also be performed. Holm correction will be applied within each correlational block.

Qualitative analyses will include chi-square tests, one-way ANOVAs, and Spearman correlations. Planned analyses include preference for the Bio-enhanced version across SES groups, frequency of biophilic mentions across SES groups, associations between qualitative mentions and fixation measures, and associations between word valence and Positive Affect (PANAS).

Significant ANOVA effects will be followed by Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons. For Neighborhood SES, comparisons will include Low vs. Medium, Low vs. High, and Medium vs. High. For significant Condition × Neighborhood SES interactions, pairwise comparisons will be conducted within each SES level.

Assumptions will be evaluated through inspection of Q-Q plots of residuals. Outliers will be defined as observations exceeding ±3 SD from the mean for the relevant variable and will be retained if they reflect genuine variability. Effect sizes will be reported as partial eta-squared (η²p) for ANOVA effects, Cohen’s d for pairwise comparisons, Cramér’s V for chi-square tests, and Spearman’s ρ for correlations. The significance threshold will be α = .05.
table.transformations: No transformations will be applied to the data. All variables will be used in their original units as described in the Variables section. For correlational analyses, delta scores will be computed for variables measured in both conditions as Bio-enhanced − Original. Neighborhood SES will be coded ordinally (1 = Low, 2 = Medium, 3 = High) for the correlational analyses in Block B.
table.inference_criteria: Statistical significance will be evaluated using α = .05. Holm correction will be applied to pairwise comparisons and within each family of correlational analyses. Effect sizes will be reported regardless of statistical significance, including partial eta-squared (η²p) for ANOVA effects, Cohen's d for pairwise comparisons, Cramér's V for chi-square tests, and Spearman's ρ for correlations.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: No participants will be excluded from the analysis as a whole. Outliers will be defined as values exceeding ±3 SD from the mean for the relevant variable. These values will be retained if they reflect genuine variability and will be flagged in the results. Values will be excluded only if they are identified as technical errors (e.g., eye-tracking calibration failure, tracker loss, or recording artifacts), and in such cases only the affected metric will be excluded for that participant. All exclusion decisions will be made prior to inferential testing and documented.
table.missing_data_handling: No imputation will be performed. Missing data will be reported transparently, including the number and percentage of missing values per variable and per analysis. If a participant has missing data for a specific metric, they will be excluded only from analyses involving that metric. The number of participants contributing to each analysis will be reported. Missing data patterns will be examined descriptively, and any substantial imbalance will be noted as a limitation.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Additional exploratory analyses are planned. Mixed ANOVAs will be conducted for Average Fixation Duration and Average Saccadic Velocity using the same design as the primary analyses. Separate one-way ANOVAs will examine Pure Biophilia Fixations, Urban Regeneration Fixations, Mixed Regeneration + Biophilia Fixations, and Artistic Biophilia Fixations across Neighborhood SES groups.

Exploratory correlational analyses will examine associations between changes in attention to intervention areas and affective outcomes, visual exploration of biophilic elements and affective responses, and attentional orienting measures (Time to First Fixation and First Fixation Duration) and affective or evaluative outcomes. Holm correction will be applied within each exploratory family of analyses.

Additional qualitative analyses will include thematic coding, descriptive summaries, chi-square tests, one-way ANOVAs, and Spearman correlations integrating qualitative responses with eye-tracking and affective measures. Any analyses not specified as confirmatory will be clearly labeled as exploratory.

text.text: Inequity in access to urban green spaces perpetuates marked disparities in psychological wellbeing in cities.

The present study evaluates whether micro-scale biophilic interventions in virtual environments act as a socio-perceptual equalizer (Environmental Equigenesis Hypothesis) and modulate attention through oculomotor patterns of soft fascination (Attention Restoration Theory).
Within this framework, 60 Hz eye-tracking integrated into Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) was used to capture implicit attentional dynamics objectively.

Framed within a mixed methods project registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) after data collection and before any inferential analysis, and given the density of the data obtained, this manuscript reports exclusively the quantitative block focused on oculomotor and psychometric triangulation, reserving the qualitative analysis for a subsequent report.
A sample of 75 participants exposed to 360° virtual tours evaluated low-, medium-, and high-socioeconomic-status (SES) neighborhoods under Original and Enhanced conditions.

Eye-tracking revealed that the biophilic design did not alter the total volume of fixations but significantly reduced the average fixation duration, a pattern compatible with the attentional coupling of soft fascination.
In parallel, subjective increases in positive affect, liking, esthetic evaluation, and relaxation were observed, while perceived stress did not change significantly overall.

No significant differences in esthetic evaluation between neighborhoods remained after the intervention, and the areas-of-interest (AOIs) metrics showed a different allocation of gaze across neighborhoods, partly because the interventions applied were not the same in each one.
Eye-tracking complemented the self-report data, although the main equigenesis findings rest on the psychometric measures.
Accelerated global urbanization has redefined patterns of human settlement, progressively replacing natural infrastructure with dense, highly mineralized built environments.

This transformation has not only intensified the physical and psychological disconnection between the population and natural ecosystems but has also positioned itself as a major determinant in the growing prevalence of cognitive fatigue, chronic stress, and affective disorders in cities (Beatley, 2016; Wolch et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This transformation has not only intensified the physical and psychological disconnection between the population and natural ecosystems but has also positioned itself as a major determinant in the growing prevalence of cognitive fatigue, chronic stress, and affective disorders in cities <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Beatley, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Wolch et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, the impacts of environmental deprivation are not distributed uniformly across the urban matrix; on the contrary, socio-spatial segregation perpetuates profound environmental inequity.

Neighborhoods with lower socioeconomic status (SES) systematically face lower vegetation coverage, lower-quality parks, and greater exposure to physical and social stressors, drastically reducing daily opportunities for psychological restoration (Galera et al., 2025; Mitchell and Popham, 2008; Rigolon et al., 2018; Xian et al., 2024).

text.text: In this scenario, biophilic design, the intentional incorporation of nature, biological patterns, and organic forms into the built environment (Kellert, 2018; Ryan et al., 2014), emerges as a strategic urban intervention with high potential for promoting mental health and social equity.
text.formatted: In this scenario, biophilic design, the intentional incorporation of nature, biological patterns, and organic forms into the built environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Kellert, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Ryan et al., 2014)</ref>, emerges as a strategic urban intervention with high potential for promoting mental health and social equity.

text.text: The theoretical body of environmental psychology offers two complementary conceptual frameworks to explain the mechanisms underlying environmental restoration.

On the one hand, Attention Restoration Theory (ART; Kaplan and Kaplan, 1989; Kaplan, 1995) posits that conventional urban environments demand constant effort of directed attention (top-down mechanism), which is susceptible to depletion and cognitive fatigue.
text.formatted: On the one hand, Attention Restoration Theory (ART; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kaplan and Kaplan, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kaplan, 1995)</ref> posits that conventional urban environments demand constant effort of directed attention (top-down mechanism), which is susceptible to depletion and cognitive fatigue.

text.text: Exposure to natural elements, in contrast, recruits involuntary attention or "soft fascination," a low-effort visual processing that allows for the recovery of attentional capacity.

On the other hand, Stress Recovery Theory (SRT; Ulrich, 1983; Ulrich et al., 1991) holds that primary visual contact with organic patterns triggers an immediate positive and nonspecific affective response, modulating autonomic nervous system reactivity and attenuating sympathetic alertness without requiring complex prior cognitive elaboration.
text.formatted: On the other hand, Stress Recovery Theory (SRT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Ulrich, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Ulrich et al., 1991)</ref> holds that primary visual contact with organic patterns triggers an immediate positive and nonspecific affective response, modulating autonomic nervous system reactivity and attenuating sympathetic alertness without requiring complex prior cognitive elaboration.

text.text: Despite the solid empirical support for ART and SRT, the interaction between the restorative benefits of biophilic design and the socioeconomic inequity of the urban environment continues to raise crucial questions.

The Equigenesis Hypothesis (Mitchell and Popham, 2008) suggests that restorative environmental resources can operate as a "socio-perceptual equalizer," exerting a disproportionately stronger buffering impact on vulnerable communities.
text.formatted: The Equigenesis Hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Mitchell and Popham, 2008)</ref> suggests that restorative environmental resources can operate as a "socio-perceptual equalizer," exerting a disproportionately stronger buffering impact on vulnerable communities.

text.text: In low-SES communities, characterized by prolonged green deprivation, the incorporation of biophilic interventions may generate a higher marginal gain compared with affluent neighborhoods, where daily environmental resources attenuate the margin of improvement (ceiling effect); we refer to this idea here as a basal restorative deficit.

However, most research on equigenesis has analyzed macro-scale green infrastructure (such as peri-urban parks or protected areas), leaving a substantial gap regarding whether micro-scale biophilic interventions (such as the integration of vegetation on facades, vertical gardens, and organic-themed urban art) succeed in equalizing esthetic and affective evaluations on urban streets with different degrees of baseline degradation.

It should be noted that in the present design the participants are not residents of the neighborhoods they evaluate, so what varies is the baseline quality of the scene and not the observer's own environmental deprivation.

At the methodological level, the evaluation of landscape perception has historically faced the tension between the ecological validity of field studies, (with limited control of environmental confounding variables), and the rigidity of static photographs in the laboratory (Browning et al., 2020; Dupont et al., 2014; Higuera-Trujillo et al., 2017).
text.formatted: At the methodological level, the evaluation of landscape perception has historically faced the tension between the ecological validity of field studies, (with limited control of environmental confounding variables), and the rigidity of static photographs in the laboratory <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Browning et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Dupont et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Higuera-Trujillo et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The development of Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) combined with eye-tracking technologies has overcome this dilemma, offering a platform of high perceptual fidelity and rigorous experimental control (Ferreira et al., 2025; Finkler et al., 2025; Frost et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2024; Mostajeran et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The development of Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) combined with eye-tracking technologies has overcome this dilemma, offering a platform of high perceptual fidelity and rigorous experimental control <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ferreira et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Finkler et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Frost et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Jin et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Mostajeran et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Weng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Through immersive 360° videos, IVR allows participants to be placed in dynamic three-dimensional urban tours, while eye-tracking objectively records gaze behavior in real time.

Metric by metric, the analysis of Total Fixation Count, Average Fixation Duration, Average Saccadic Velocity, and the count of selective fixations on areas of interest (AOI Fixation Count) offers a direct neurocognitive window to unravel the mechanism of the 'nature gaze' (Fleming et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Metric by metric, the analysis of Total Fixation Count, Average Fixation Duration, Average Saccadic Velocity, and the count of selective fixations on areas of interest (AOI Fixation Count) offers a direct neurocognitive window to unravel the mechanism of the 'nature gaze' <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Fleming et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This allows discerning whether the psychological benefit responds to a quantitative exploratory overload or to the establishment of a pattern of 'soft fascination' characterized by distributed, agile, and selective attentional processing of organic components.

As a direct antecedent of this line of research, our group conducted an exploratory pilot study (N = 16; Ferreira et al., 2026) that demonstrated the methodological feasibility of integrating IVR and eye-tracking to capture socio-perceptual responses to biophilic transformations in neighborhoods with different socioeconomic levels.
text.formatted: As a direct antecedent of this line of research, our group conducted an exploratory pilot study <ref type="bibr">(N = 16;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Ferreira et al., 2026)</ref> that demonstrated the methodological feasibility of integrating IVR and eye-tracking to capture socio-perceptual responses to biophilic transformations in neighborhoods with different socioeconomic levels.

text.text: The preliminary results of the pilot provided initial empirical evidence in favor of equigenesis in the perceptual domain: whereas in the baseline scenario (Original) there was a marked esthetic gradient favoring high-SES environments, the biophilic intervention exerted a social equalization effect (ηp² = .41 for both liking and esthetic evaluation), raising the ratings of the most disadvantaged neighborhoods to equate them with those of affluent environments.

However, the pilot study also revealed an oculomotor paradox: enriched low-SES scenes triggered the highest volume of fixations (M = 462.6) and visual coverage (M = 48.78%), and low-SES scenes showed higher saccadic velocity than the other scenes in both conditions (a main effect of SES, not of the intervention).

This pattern was tentatively interpreted as novelty-motivated arousal, suggesting a dissociation between conscious affective improvement and physiological stress recovery that requires a longer exposure time.

Despite its valuable methodological contributions, the pilot study had a small sample size (N = 16), employed some single-item scales, and lacked a pre-specified differentiation between confirmatory and exploratory variables.

To overcome these limitations and provide robust empirical verification, the present study scales the 3 × 2 factorial design of the pilot, which was fully within-subjects, to a mixed design with an independently calculated sample of N = 75 participants, with a distinction between confirmatory and exploratory hypotheses registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) platform after data collection and before analysis.

The AOI scheme was also changed with respect to the pilot, and the protocol differed in other respects (participants now viewed the tours standing with free body rotation rather than seated, and each tour comprised six instead of ten scenes).

Absolute oculomotor values, including AOI counts and saccadic velocity, are therefore not directly comparable between the two studies, and the present analyses rely on within-study contrasts between conditions and neighborhoods.

The study evaluates, confirmatory and exploratory, how micro-scale biophilic interventions modulate affect, esthetic evaluation, and oculomotor dynamics in Low, Medium, and High SES neighborhoods in the city of Almería (Spain).

Five main hypotheses, as specified in the OSF registration, are formulated: H1 (General effect of biophilia): Scenes enriched with biophilic design will significantly increase positive affect (PANAS Positive Affect), liking (Liking), esthetic evaluation (Esthetic Evaluation), subjective relaxation (Relaxation), and patterns of global visual engagement (Total Fixation Count) (assessed both globally and selectively) compared with unmodified original urban scenes.

The marginal psychological benefit (affective and evaluative) produced by the biophilic intervention will be significantly greater in the low-SES neighborhood context compared with the medium and high SES contexts, with biophilia acting as a socio-perceptual equalizer of public space.

The volume of fixations directed at the specific intervention areas (AOI Fixation Count) will experience a significantly more pronounced increase in low-SES scenes after the incorporation of biophilic elements.

Exposure to biophilic design will immediately increase positive affect and the subjective sensation of relaxation, but will not induce a simultaneous immediate reduction in perceived stress (Perceived Stress) or an alteration in oculomotor arousal dynamics (Average Saccadic Velocity).

The exploration time focused specifically on natural and organic artistic elements (Fixations on Added Vegetation, Fixations on Biophilic Art), accompanied by shorter and more fluid fixation patterns (Average Fixation Duration, a marker of soft fascination according to ART), will correlate positively with the increase in positive affect and esthetic appreciation.
The sample consisted of university students from the University of Almería (UAL), recruited through public calls disseminated via the university's institutional online portal.
The final evaluated sample comprised N = 75 valid participants.
Regarding gender distribution, 89.3% (n = 67) were women, 9.3% (n = 7) were men, and 1.3% (n = 1) preferred not to specify their gender.
Regarding participant age, the median was 19 years, with an age range between 17 and 43 years.
Participants were assigned to one of three neighborhood socioeconomic status levels (Low SES: n = 24; Medium SES: n = 26; High SES: n = 25).
The sample size was determined a priori through a power analysis in G*Power 3.1 for a mixed ANOVA 3 × 2 (one between-subjects factor: Neighborhood SES; one within-subject factor: Design Condition).

Assuming a level α = .05, a power (1 -β) = .80, a correlation between repeated measures of .50, nonsphericity correction ε = 1, and a small-to-medium effect size of f = 0.20, the calculation indicated a minimum required sample of N = 66 participants (with df = 63 in the denominator for the Condition × SES interaction).
To prevent loss of power derived from experimental mortality or oculomotor calibration failures, the sample was oversampled by 14%, reaching the target figure of 75 participants.

To guarantee methodological validity and participant safety during immersion in virtual reality and oculomotor recording, the following exclusion criteria were applied: presenting a self-reported history of severe motion sickness, color blindness or achromatopsia, neurological alterations, or any other medical condition that could interfere with the safe use of the VR headset or affect performance in the evaluation tasks.
Regarding inclusion criteria, only normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity was determined.
The study employed a mixed factorial design 3 × 2.

The between-subjects factor referred to Neighborhood SES (3 levels: Low, Medium, and High), classified from the tertiles of average income by postal code and municipality published by the National Statistics Institute (INE).
On the other hand, the within-subject factor consisted of the Design Condition (2 levels: Original vs.
Enhanced).
Each participant observed a single neighborhood in both conditions.
One block per SES level was used, so Neighborhood SES is confounded with the specific streets of each block.
The order of presentation of the conditions was randomized through simple assignment, and the assignment of neighborhood SES was counterbalanced among participants.
The study was approved by the Human Research Bioethics Committee of the University of Almería (Ref.
UALBIO2026_016; date: 7 May 2026).
All participants signed the informed consent prior to the start of the sessions.
Data were collected between 15 May and 30 June 2026.

The study was registered on the OSF (preregistration for studies with existing data) after data collection and before any descriptive or inferential analysis of the final dataset (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3TCWR ).

text.text: The stimuli consisted of immersive virtual tours based on 360° videos with a fixed viewpoint.
The original recording was captured at 8K resolution using an Insta360 X4 camera under homogeneous morning lighting.
Each condition was composed of a tour of six sequential 360° videos of approximately one minute each (total exposure time ≈ 6 minutes per tour).
The Enhanced versions maintained exactly the same geometry and perspective as the Original Scenes.

In the enhanced versions, micro-scale interventions were applied that included: addition of vegetation (trees, shrubs, planters, and green facades), organic-themed artistic murals, digital facade cleaning, and elimination of visual degradation elements (such as graffiti and overhead wiring).
The interventions were adapted to each neighborhood, and the type and number of intervened AOIs were not equivalent across neighborhoods.

The six videos per neighborhood are a subset of the footage recorded for the pilot study (Ferreira et al., 2026), in which comparable enhancement proportions were targeted across neighborhoods (approximately +25% green pixel density and +15% esthetically treated surface area).
text.formatted: The six videos per neighborhood are a subset of the footage recorded for the pilot study <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ferreira et al., 2026)</ref>, in which comparable enhancement proportions were targeted across neighborhoods (approximately +25% green pixel density and +15% esthetically treated surface area).

text.text: Those proportions are reported for the full pilot set and are not reported separately for the six-video subset analyzed here; moreover, the type and number of discrete interventions, and therefore of intervened AOIs, differed between neighborhoods.
The immersive presentation and real-time oculomotor recording were carried out using Meta Quest Pro headsets through the SightLab VR platform (WorldViz) over the OpenXR protocol.
The system recorded eye-tracking data at a sampling frequency of 60 Hz (one sample every ≈16.7 ms).
To maximize ecological validity and reduce experimental fatigue, the headset's stored calibration profile was used together with automatic slippage correction algorithms.

Oculomotor data processing employed the velocity-threshold identification algorithm (I-VT): fixations were defined as periods with gaze velocity below 30°/s lasting a minimum of 100 ms, while saccades were identified as movements above said threshold.

Following the guidelines of the OSF registration, the measured variables were categorized according to their analytical role: The single-item scales (Liking, Esthetic Evaluation, Relaxation, Perceived Stress, Interest) were developed for this study and are not formally validated.
The experimental procedure was developed following a rigorously standardized and sequential protocol.
Upon arrival at the laboratory, participants were received, compliance with inclusion criteria was verified, and they signed the corresponding informed consent.
Next, each participant was assigned in a counterbalanced manner to one of the three neighborhood socioeconomic levels (Low, Medium, or High SES).
Subsequently, the Meta Quest Pro virtual reality headset was adjusted and the eye-tracking profile was verified to guarantee optimal oculomotor recording.
The testing phase began with exposure to the first experimental condition (Original or Enhanced, randomized among participants), consisting of a tour through six immersive 360° videos.

During visualization, participants remained standing at a fixed central anchor area; free 360° body rotation was allowed for free exploration of the environment, but translational displacement was restricted to preserve consistency of the viewpoint.
Advancement through the scenes was controlled directly by the participant using the hand controller, so viewing time was self-paced.
Throughout the immersive tour, the system continuously recorded gaze dynamics at a sampling frequency of 60 Hz.

At the end of the first condition, participants removed the headset and immediately completed the post-exposure questionnaire battery, which included the PANAS scale, ad hoc evaluative items, and open-response questions.
A 5-minute washout interval was then applied using a neutral distractor task to prevent emotional or attentional carryover effects between conditions.

Next, participants completed exposure to the second experimental condition under the same posture, body rotation, and oculomotor recording protocol, followed by a second administration of the questionnaire package.
The session concluded with a debriefing phase and closure of the procedure.

Although the study's registration on the Open Science Framework (OSF) originally proposed a mixed-methods approach integrating this quantitative oculomotor evaluation with the qualitative analysis of post-exposure open responses, the high density and complexity of the data advised delimiting the scope of this first manuscript.

In order to rigorously deepen the oculomotor and psychometric indicators, this submission focuses exclusively on the quantitative dimension supported by eye-tracking, while the qualitative corpus will be reported in a subsequent independent publication.
All statistical analyses were executed under a prefixed significance level of α = .05 using JASP v0.98.8 software.

A mixed ANOVA 3 × 2 was applied to each of the 7 main confirmatory variables (PANAS Positive Affect, Liking, Esthetic Evaluation, Relaxation, Perceived Stress, AOI Fixation Count, and Total Fixation Count), including Individual SES as a covariate.
The model evaluated the main effects of Condition, Neighborhood SES, the critical Condition × SES interaction, and the covariate effects.

The covariate was entered without centering, so the main effects of Condition in these models are conditional on a covariate value of 0 and may understate the raw mean differences shown in Tables 2 and 3; the interpretation therefore relies mainly on the Condition × SES interactions and on the Holm-corrected within-group comparisons.

Effect sizes are reported as partial eta-squared (ηp²) for ANOVAs and Spearman's ρ for correlations.

Deviations from the registration: Kruskal-Wallis and Wilcoxon tests were used for the intervention subcomponents and for the two skewed latency variables (Time to First Fixation, First Fixation Duration).

The registration expected a positive association between fixation duration and affective gains in Block E, whereas the interpretation of shorter fixations as a marker of soft fascination in this manuscript is post hoc.

The findings of this study suggest that the integration of micro-scale biophilic design elements in virtual urban environments is associated with improvements in participants' subjective evaluations, accompanied by differentiated visual scanning patterns.

In line with Hypothesis 1 (H1) for the subjective measures, the presence of vegetation and organic art was linked to higher mean scores in positive affect (F(1, 71) = 9.395, p = .003, ηp² = .117), liking (F(1, 71) = 12.71, p < .001, ηp² = .152), esthetic appreciation (F(1, 71) = 25.28, p < .001, ηp² = .263), and subjective relaxation (F(1, 71) = 11.75, p = .001, ηp² = .142).

text.text: However, the absence of significant differences in Total Fixation Count between conditions (p = .213, ηp² = .022) and the lack of correlation between global exploratory volume and affective deltas (ρ ≤ .042, p ≥ .720) indicate that these benefits would not appear to depend on a quantitative increase in spatial scanning (counts were not normalized by viewing time, which was self-paced).

On the other hand, the decrease observed in average fixation duration, which decreased from 0.241 s in the Original condition to 0.224 s in the Enhanced one (F(1, 71) = 9.686, p = .003, ηp² = .120), constitutes an oculomotor pattern compatible with the phenomenon of soft fascination, a fundamental pillar of Attention Restoration Theory (ART; Kaplan and Kaplan, 1989; Kaplan, 1995).

Support for H2 is therefore partial: the interaction was significant for positive affect and esthetic evaluation, but not for liking, relaxation or perceived stress; the interaction for positive affect would not survive a correction across the seven confirmatory models; and the similar esthetic ratings after the intervention (close to the top of the scale) reflect a nonsignificant difference and not a demonstration of equivalence.

Moreover, since participants were not residents of these neighborhoods, the results describe how scenes of different baseline quality respond to the same kind of intervention, and not the effect on people living in deprived environments.

The analysis of the intervention subcomponents reflects that the allocation of gaze toward different typologies of urban renewal differed across neighborhoods.

The higher volume of fixations on pure vegetation in the low socioeconomic level group (M = 302.1; H(2) = 21.90, p < .001) is compatible with the idea that vegetation acts as a high-salience restorative stimulus in landscapes with an initial green scarcity.

This reflects the current AOI coding of mural elements rather than a difference in attention across neighborhoods and will be addressed in a revised version.

In contrast, the greater focus toward pure physical urban regeneration elements in the medium socioeconomic level (M = 34.88; p < .001) or toward mixed regeneration with vegetation in the high level (M = 84.52; p < .001) may indicate an exploration oriented toward the quality of built finishes and their integration with the landscape (Ferreira et al., 2026).

text.text: Because the type and number of interventions were not the same in the three neighborhoods, these patterns partly reflect the stimuli themselves, and they should be tested in a design that applies the same interventions everywhere and normalizes the counts by AOI number or size.
Regarding Hypothesis 4 (H4), the results only partly agree with a dissociation between the subjective affective response and stress recovery.

Participants reported a greater sensation of subjective relaxation in the Enhanced condition (F (1, 71) = 11.75, p = .001, ηp² = .142), while the overall effect of condition on perceived stress (p = .209, ηp² = .022) and on average saccadic velocity as an oculomotor indicator of arousal (p = .692, ηp² = .002) was not significant, and these two changes were not correlated (ρ = -.056).

However, mean stress ratings were lower in the Enhanced condition in the three groups, and the reduction was significant in the low SES group (p Holm = .003), with ratings close to the floor of the scale, so the absence of an overall effect should not be taken as evidence that stress did not change.

This observation can be related to the theoretical distinction between the immediate affective responses postulated by Stress Recovery Theory (SRT; Ulrich, 1983; Ulrich et al., 1991) and the cognitive and physiological restoration processes contemplated in ART (Kaplan, 1995).

text.text: Similarly, the stability observed in the nonparametric metrics of initial orientation (Time to First Fixation: p = .445; First Fixation Duration: p = .465) indicates that the attentional benefits of biophilia would not respond to an automatic bottom-up capture bias in the first milliseconds, but rather to a distributed processing throughout the immersion.
Compared with the pilot study (Ferreira et al., 2026), which used a fully within-subjects design with 16 participants, the present results replicate some findings and not others.

text.text: The convergence of esthetic evaluations across neighborhoods after the intervention was observed in both studies (interaction η²p = .41 in the pilot and .18 here), as were the main effect of the intervention on relaxation without a Condition × SES interaction and the absence of an overall effect on perceived stress.
In contrast, the Condition × SES interaction for liking found in the pilot was not observed here, whereas an interaction for positive affect, absent in the pilot, emerged in the present sample.

Among the oculomotor indices, the effect of the intervention on average fixation duration, which did not reach significance in the pilot, was significant here, while the association between changes in saccadic velocity and changes in relaxation reported in the pilot was not replicated.

Given the differences in design, sample size, viewing posture and AOI scheme, the most consistent result across both studies is the esthetic convergence, whereas the affective and oculomotor patterns require confirmation in larger and more diverse samples.

From the perspective of urban planning and biophilic design (Beatley, 2016; Kellert, 2018; Ryan et al., 2014), these findings suggest that micro-scale interventions represent a promising strategy for improving the perceptual quality of public space in disadvantaged neighborhoods.

text.text: However, when considering their translation into public health policies (Wolch et al., 2014), it must be borne in mind that the mitigation of perceived stress would potentially require continued daily exposures and integrated green itineraries.

text.text: Among the limitations of this study is the composition of a university sample with a high percentage of women (89.3%) and a median age of 19 years, which advises caution before extrapolating the results to other age or clinical groups.
Likewise, passive exposure via 360-degree video with a fixed viewpoint in virtual reality limits active translational exploration.
Only one block per SES level was used and the interventions were not equivalent across neighborhoods, so SES is confounded with the specific streets and with the type of intervention.

Fixations on Biophilic Art depend on an AOI coding scheme that was not applied uniformly across neighborhoods; results involving this variable are preliminary and will be revised in a subsequent version.
The single-item scales are not validated and are strongly intercorrelated, perceived stress and negative affect show floor effects, and there was no pre-exposure measure of affect.
The eye-tracking was recorded at 60 Hz without recalibration, and fixation counts were not normalized by the self-paced viewing time.

In addition, individual SES was entered as an uncentered covariate, which may understate the main effects of condition, seven confirmatory models were tested at α = .05 without correction across models, and the exploratory correlations were not adjusted for SES.

Future research using immersive virtual reality and eye-tracking (Finkler et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2024; Mostajeran et al., 2025) should evaluate the impact of these interventions in real scenarios or with free navigation, with several blocks per SES level and identical interventions, incorporating complementary neurophysiological recordings over longer exposure periods.

text.text: Finally, in terms of methodological scope, it should be recalled that the design registered on OSF contemplated the collection of qualitative data through open questions after each virtual tour.

Due to the extension and complexity of the quantitative findings presented in this work, it was deliberately decided to divide the research report into two phases; the subsequent publication of the qualitative corpus will allow complementing the oculomotor and evaluative pattern described here, deepening the experiences and meanings attributed by participants to the biophilic transformation of the environment.

The evidence observed in this sample indicates that the incorporation of micro-scale biophilic interventions in virtual environments was not accompanied by an increase in the global exploratory volume of the scene (Total Fixation Count: ηp² = .022) and was associated with a small reduction in average fixation duration (ηp² = .120), which is compatible with, but not specific to, the soft fascination mechanism characteristic of the attentional restoration processes postulated by the environmental psychology literature.

The results show trends congruent with the environmental equigenesis hypothesis for positive affect and esthetic evaluation, highlighting an increase in positive affect that reached statistical significance exclusively in the lowest socioeconomic level neighborhood (Δ = +9.80 points) and the disappearance of significant differences in esthetic evaluation between unequal urban contexts, reducing the initial gap until reaching similar post-intervention averages (M ≈ 4.04-4.16).
The interaction was not significant for liking, relaxation or perceived stress.
For its part, the elevation in liking manifested cross-sectionally among socioeconomic levels (ηp² = .152), suggesting a generalized interest toward the integration of nature in the city.

Biophilic immersion induced an increase in serenity and subjective relaxation (ηp² = .142), whereas the overall effect on perceived stress (ηp² = .022) and on saccadic arousal indicators (ηp² = .002) was not significant.

Perceived stress did decrease significantly in the lowest socioeconomic level neighborhood, so the proposed dissociation between conscious affect and perceived stress is not clearly supported, and whether the recovery of latent stress requires longer or continued exposures remains an open question.

The allocation of gaze toward the renewed elements differed between neighborhoods: observers exposed to the disadvantaged scenes directed more fixations toward pure vegetation (M = 302.1 fixations), whereas in the affluent sectors the scanning was oriented mostly toward the integration of architectural and natural elements (M = 84.52 fixations).
These patterns should be interpreted in light of the interventions applied in each neighborhood.

text.text: Each of the 6 videos contained 12 predefined Areas of Interest (AOIs) (72 AOIs per condition; 144 AOIs processed per participant).
Each AOI was manually classified along two independent dimensions of 5 codes each: Original Scenery (OS): OS = 1 (CEL): Constructive elements/facades.
OS = 2 (SKY): Sky area.
OS = 3 (SNE): Pre-existing vegetation.
OS = 4 (CEN): Constructive element + pre-existing vegetation.
OS = 5 (OTH): Other urban elements (vehicles, street furniture, cables).
Biophilic Intervention (BI): BI = 1 (CNT): Control (no change between conditions).
BI = 2 (BIO): Pure added vegetation.
BI = 3 (RGN): Physical urban regeneration without vegetation.
BI = 4 (RBI): Physical regeneration + added vegetation.
BI = 5 (BIA): Biophilic art (nature-themed murals).

For the intervention subcomponents (Fixations on Added Vegetation, Fixations on Physical Regeneration, Fixations on Mixed Regeneration with Vegetation, and Fixations on Biophilic Art), existing only in the Enhanced condition, one-factor between-subjects ANOVAs (Neighborhood SES) or their nonparametric alternatives (Kruskal-Wallis) were performed according to distribution assumptions.

Correlational Blocks (Deltas Δ = Enhanced -Original): Correlations (Pearson or Spearman) were structured into theoretical blocks: Block A (Confirmatory triangulation H1): ΔTotal Fixation Count vs. affective and evaluative deltas.
Block B (Confirmatory triangulation H2): Neighborhood SES vs. affective, evaluative, and attentional deltas.
Block C (Exploratory): ΔAOI Fixation Count vs. subjective deltas.
Block D (Confirmatory triangulation H4): ΔAverage Saccadic Velocity vs.
ΔPerceived Stress, ΔRelaxation, and ΔPANAS Positive Affect.
Block E (Exploratory H5): Count of fixations on specific biophilic elements and ΔAverage Fixation Duration vs. affective/evaluative deltas.
Block F (Free exploratory): Initial orientation metrics (ΔTime to First Fixation, ΔFirst Fixation Duration) vs. subjective responses.
